title: Two Loops, One Inside the Other: Cascade Control and a Speed Limit You Do Not Have to Enforce

questions.question: A single position loop with PID overshot a 2 radian move by 14.2 percent and took 3.18 seconds to settle. Why?
options: The proportional gain was too high
The derivative gain was too low
Noise
The motor was saturated through the large move and the integral wound up, and had to be unwound on the far side
questions.explanation: The cascade did not overshoot and settled in 0.81 s, with the integral in the speed loop where a large move does not wind it up.

questions.question: In a cascade, what does the outer loop output and what does the inner loop take as its setpoint?
options: A position
An acceleration
A speed: the outer loop is a gain times the position error clamped to a speed limit, and that is the inner loop's setpoint
A torque, which the inner loop limits
questions.explanation: That is why the speed limit is built in: the inner loop is never asked for more than the clamp allows.

questions.question: The cascade peaked at 3.04 rad/s against a limit of 3. Why not exactly 3?
options: The inner loop is a tracking loop and overshoots its setpoint a little
A rounding error
The limit is approximate by design
The torque limit
questions.explanation: A limit that must never be exceeded needs a hard stop behind it. The limit is not enforced afterwards. It holds because the loop is not asked for more, to within what the inner loop tracks.

questions.question: Why does the integral stop accumulating when the motor is saturated and the error is still pushing the same way?
options: The error is zero then
It would only grow without changing the torque, and then have to be unwound before the loop could respond
Integrals are unstable above a limit
To save computation
questions.explanation: Windup. Five seconds against a stuck joint left the guarded integral at 0.000 where an unguarded one would be 15.

questions.question: A load of 5 N m arrives. The P and D loop sagged 0.0250 rad for good, the PID reached 0.0208 rad worst, and the cascade 0.0051. Why is the cascade so much better?
options: The speed loop is fast and has the integral
A better motor
The load is smaller
A larger gain
questions.explanation: A load is corrected at its rate and not at the position loop's, and it finishes on target. The PID's integral is slow and shares its gain with the position loop. The cascade's is in the loop that feels the load first.

questions.question: Why must the inner loop be much faster than the outer one?
options: It does not have to be
To save memory
Otherwise the outer loop sees the inner loop's lag as a delay of its own, which cuts the gain it can have, as lesson 14-07 priced
The outer loop is slower by law
questions.explanation: Roughly a factor of ten or more. Here the inner loop's bandwidth is about 80 rad/s against the outer loop's 10.
